title: 'This is what I've always wanted to do' - Slough woman, 25, takes over village pub

It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A hospitality professional from Slough has achieved her ambition of running a pub after becoming co-owner of The Stag in Flackwell Heath. Sophie Bartlett, 25, and her partner Dan Roth, 30, have taken over the village venue, where they hope to build a community-focused business centred on good food, warm service and local support. Sophie Bartlett and Dan Roth now co-run the Stag in Flackwell Heath (Image: NQ) Originally from Slough, Miss Bartlett began her hospitality career at The Queen's Head in Little Marlow before progressing through several respected venues across the region. Despite earning a degree in economics from Cambridge University, she chose to pursue a future in hospitality rather than take up corporate career opportunities. Miss Bartlett said: "I absolutely love the industry. “I had opportunities to do something different after university, but I always wanted to come back to hospitality." The couple have confirmed the pub will open on November 22 (Image: NQ) She added that some people are surprised by her career choice. "I think people sometimes assume you're only working in hospitality while you look for something else. "That's never been the case for me. This is what I've always wanted to do." After working at The Queen's Head, she moved into a hotel environment at De Vere Beaumont Estate in Old Windsor before eventually joining the Belgian Arms in Holyport, where she met Dan. While hotels offered valuable experience, she said village pubs provided something unique. She said: “The thing I missed most was the connection with people. "In a pub, you get to know regulars and their families. You become part of people's lives and that's really special." More recently, the couple helped run The Beehive in White Waltham, where Miss Bartlett oversaw the restaurant, events and customer experience. The two are feeling positive for the future (Image: NQ) The venue went on to win a Muddy Stilettos award for Best Local, a recognition she says reflects the type of environment they want to create at The Stag.  She added: “It's about finding that balance. "You want somewhere people can celebrate a birthday, enjoy a Sunday roast or just pop in for a pint after work. That's what makes a great village pub." The pub is from the 1890s (Image: NQ) Now settled into their first business as owners, Miss Bartlett hopes The Stag can become a valued part of community life. She said: "We want people to feel welcome from the moment they walk through the door. “We want this to feel like everybody's pub, not just ours."
